Action Plan:
1) Acute asthma symptoms: Increase brown preventer inhaler (Clenil/beclomethasone) to 4 puffs twice daily until review.
2) Reliever use: Use blue salbutamol inhaler as needed for symptoms; may use as often as every 2 hours temporarily. Frequent need indicates poor control and need for urgent review.
3) Safety-net: If breathing worsens or symptoms are severe despite inhalers, go to the Emergency Department (ED) without waiting for the GP appointment.
4) Follow-up: Book a face-to-face GP appointment within the next few days for chest examination and peak flow assessment. Depending on findings, you may need antibiotics and/or oral steroids.
5) Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Reason for visit: Shortness of breath with wheeze and cough for 2–3 days.
- HPI:
  - Onset after running with a friend; could not converse while running.
  - Now dyspnea with brisk walking; wheeze and cough.
  - No sputum.
  - Blue inhaler (salbutamol) provides little relief; using daily and sometimes prophylactically.
  - Preventer (brown inhaler, Clenil/beclomethasone) used twice daily; dose not clearly documented.
  - No prior asthma hospitalizations; last asthma attack 3–4 years ago; never used oral steroids.
  - Last asthma review ~2 years ago.
  - Peak flow: Does it occasionally; has not checked since onset. Baseline when well reported around 380 L/min.
- Past medical history: Asthma; hay fever. Possible eczema (patient suspects; family history positive).
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol inhaler (blue) PRN; currently used daily and sometimes prophylactically; dose/route/frequency not fully documented.
  - Clenil (beclomethasone) brown inhaler preventer twice daily; exact dose not documented; advised to increase to 4 puffs twice daily.
  - Cetraben topical; hydrocortisone topical for skin.
- Family history: Brother with asthma; sister with eczema.
- Social history: Physically active (running). Smoking status not discussed.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies. Seasonal allergic rhinitis (hay fever).

Objective:
- Telehealth consultation; no vitals or physical examination performed.
- Respiratory: No in-person chest exam completed.
- Investigations: None performed during visit.
- Patient-reported baseline peak flow when well: ~380 L/min (per recall).

Assessment & Plan:
1. Acute shortness of breath with wheeze in known asthma:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation on background of persistent asthma (DDx: “Mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation,” High).
   - Differential diagnosis (consistent with DDx):
     - Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction contributing (Medium) — onset with running; now persistent beyond exercise.
     - Allergic asthma flare from environmental allergens (Medium) — atopic history; no specific trigger identified.
     - Viral URI/acute bronchitis triggering asthma (Low-Medium) — acute onset and cough without systemic symptoms.
     - Poor inhaler technique/suboptimal controller regimen (Medium) — frequent SABA with poor relief; medication confusion; last review 2 years ago.
   - Investigations planned:
     - Face-to-face chest examination and peak flow measurement at upcoming GP visit.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Increase brown preventer (Clenil/beclomethasone) to 4 puffs twice daily.
     - Use blue salbutamol inhaler as needed for symptoms; may use as often as every 2 hours temporarily; frequent need indicates poor control.
     - Safety-net: If symptoms worsen or severe despite inhalers, attend ED immediately.
     - At follow-up, depending on exam/peak flow, may require antibiotics and/or oral steroids.
   - Relevant referrals:
     - Book face-to-face GP appointment in the next few days for assessment.

2. Atopy (hay fever; possible eczema):
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Atopic diathesis (allergic rhinitis; possible eczema). No acute management changes discussed today.
   - Differential diagnosis: Not applicable.
   - Investigations planned: None discussed.
   - Treatment planned: Continue current topical cetraben and hydrocortisone as previously used (dose/route/frequency not documented).
   - Relevant referrals: None discussed.

Quality checks:
- Missing/expected elements:
  - No vitals, pulse oximetry, or in-visit peak flow obtained.
  - Smoking status, pregnancy status (if relevant), recent infection or exposure history, and red-flag screening (e.g., chest pain, hemoptysis) not documented.
  - Exact inhaler doses and technique not confirmed; full medication reconciliation incomplete.
  - Immunization status (including COVID-19) not discussed.
- Internal conflicts:
  - Patient initially said “I have a fever,” then clarified “hay fever” — initial mishearing corrected; no fever ultimately reported (conflict noted).
  - Salbutamol frequency mentioned as “every 2–4 hours” earlier and “up to every 2 hours” later; final advice appears to be up to every 2 hours PRN (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: Occasional audio clarity issues and medication name confusion (e.g., “Flanel Bactroban” later clarified to Cetraben; preventer confirmed as brown Clenil).
